w: What's tested When to copy the existing bite What to check in sideways and forward movements Keeping the bite vs rebuilding it, and how to take bite records Rules for each kind of filling, crown and bridge Implants: why and how their bite is different This is where occlusion meets everyday restorative work. Patients often have problems (worn spots, cracks, loose teeth) before they have symptoms, and replacing a broken crown doesn't fix the force that broke it. Guidance and MIP Accepted bite schemes are balanced (for dentures), mutually protected, and group function. If a patient has no problems, copy the guidance they already have. MIP is where chewing ends and where you swallow, but it isn't stable long-term. Teeth touch in MIP only about 17.5 minutes a day (about 1,800 chewing strokes and 500 swallows). The ligaments around the teeth can feel something 20 microns thick. Check sideways movements for loose guiding teeth and smooth motion; a contact on the non-working side tends to steer the jaw. A patient who has lived with one for years can keep it, but don't create one. Check forward movement too: any back-tooth bumping in forward movement must be fixed before you restore the front teeth. Keep the bite or rebuild it? The conformative approach fits the new work into the existing bite, with only small local fixes (shortening a cusp that sticks down, removing a non-working contact or a deflecting spot). Use an MIP bite record. The reorganized approach rebuilds the whole bite starting from the seated joints (a CR record, taken by guiding the jaw with both hands), so you have a repeatable starting point, an even bite, and no new problems. To decide, compare where the teeth touch with the joints seated against MIP, and look for wear, cracks and loose teeth. Bite-record materials include PVS (Regisil), wax (Aluwax), zinc oxide eugenol paste, acrylic and plaster. Wax sets in a second or two; PVS takes 20-30 seconds while the patient moves. Don't put material across the whole arch, and trim it so you can check the casts sit right. For an MIP record, put material only where the teeth don't touch, trim it to the cusp tips, and keep it off the gums. With rubbery materials, keep the patient biting while it sets, trim with a scalpel, and press the models together while mounting. Back teeth Every filling should touch the opposite tooth evenly, at the same time as the other teeth. It should not be high, should not push the tooth sideways, should not be left out of contact (the teeth drift into it, never in a good way), and should not touch on sideways movements. For a big filling, first check the opposite tooth for over-eruption and fix it. Several large back fillings may need a full rebuild with strong materials. A single crown between other teeth is usually conformative, best recorded by just fitting the models together by hand, with no face-bow and a simple articulator; at try-in check that it's fully seated and the side contacts are right before checking the bite. A crown at the end of the row needs a bite record so the model doesn't tip. Three-unit bridges are usually conformative, with a good opposite bite plane and a semi-adjustable articulator. Whole quadrants may need the opposite side fixed first. A tiny hinge articulator only helps the lab, not you. Front teeth Small front fillings (Class III) copy the old contacts and keep the bite off the filling. Corner fillings (Class IV) should share contacts between filling and tooth. For one front crown, first fix any back-tooth bump that slides the jaw forward. When crowning both upper centrals or a canine, use a custom guide table; to copy the existing guidance, take its impression before trimming the teeth. If the guidance is poor, wax it up, wear temporaries for at least three weeks (months for grinders), record them, and copy them. Use "s" to check bite height: the front teeth should come within 1-2 mm. Implants An implant is fused to bone with no cushioning ligament, so it barely moves (2-3 microns down vs about 28 for a tooth). Its bite is built light: on a gentle close it barely touches, and on a hard clench it touches equally with the teeth, which sink a little. A front implant shouldn't do the canine guiding alone; it shares the load with natural teeth. A back implant should avoid contact in sideways and forward movements. Shimstock (a 12-micron strip) helps you check this.
